blocks.text: And Pliny passim, as in book 10, ch. 3, where he treats the haliaeetus: That which is born of them has its kind among the ossifrages. And a little later: Some add a kind of eagle which they call the bearded eagle; the Tuscans, however, call it the ossifrage. And again, where he speaks of the young which eagles cast out from weariness of feeding them: [II, 773] When cast out by them, the related kind of the ossifrage takes them up and rears them with its own. And in ch. 7: Some think that the immussulus is the young of the vulture, and the sanqualis that of the ossifrage. Likewise, Massurius says that the sanqualis is the ossifrage. And in book 30, ch. 7: The ossifrage has a single intestine of wonderful nature, which digests everything it has swallowed. And a little before: The dried stomach of the ossifrage, taken in drink, is most useful for those who do not digest their food. And in the chapter immediately following he prescribes the same to be taken for expelling stones. Isidore too, book 12, ch. 7: The bird that drops bones from on high and breaks them is commonly called ossifrangus (read ossifragus), whence it received its name from breaking bones. See also Festus under the words immussulus and sanqualis. In one Greek glossary ossifragus is rendered ὀστοκόπος [ostokopos], ὀστοκλάστης [ostoklastēs], ὀστοκατεάκτης [ostokateaktēs]; in another, but wrongly, ὀστοκόραξ [ostokorax]. In Dioscorides it is φίνις [phinis]: Φίνις, he says, τὸ ὄρνεον, ὃ Ῥωμαϊστὶ καλοῦσιν ὀσσίφραγον [Phinis to orneon, ho Rhōmaisti kalousin ossiphragon]. And in older writers φήνη [phēnē], a word very well known from Homer and Aristotle, which the Arabs also use. Damir, from Ibn Sida: الفينة طاير يشبه العقاب فانا خاف البرد انحدر الي اليمن [al-fīna ṭāyir yushbih al-ʿuqāb fa-anā khāfa al-bard inḥadara ilā al-Yaman], Phena, a bird like the eagle, which, when it fears the cold, sets out for Ieman, that is, for Arabia Felix. But commonly it is called, as we said, كاسر [kāsir], breaker, and كاسر اعظام [kāsir aʿẓām], breaker of bones. Likewise مكلفة [mukallafa] mechalapha, from its black colour mixed with reddish or yellowish. Damir: الكاسر العقاب [al-kāsir al-ʿuqāb], Alchasir (or breaker), a kind of eagle. The same elsewhere: كاسر العظام المكلفة [kāsir al-ʿiẓām al-mukallafa], The breaker of bones, that is, the mechalepha. And in the chapter On the mechalepha: الفرخ الذي ترمي [col. 188] به العقاب من الثلثة يحضنه طاير يقال له المكلفه ويقال له كاسر العظام وتربيه [al-farkh alladhī tarmī bihi al-ʿuqāb min al-thalātha yaḥḍunuhu ṭāyir yuqāl lahu al-mukallafa wa-yuqāl lahu kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-turabbīhi], The chick which the eagle casts out of the three is brooded and fed by a bird which is called mechalepha and breaker of bones. And in the chapter العقاب [al-ʿuqāb], or On the eagle: والعرب يسمي العقاب الكاسر [wa-al-ʿArab yusammī al-ʿuqāb al-kāsir], The Arabs also call the eagle (that is, a species of eagle) the breaker. And below: والفرخ الذي تلقيه يعطف عليه طاير يسمي كاسر العظام ويسمي المكلفه ايضا فيربيه [wa-al-farkh alladhī tulqīhi yaʿṭifu ʿalayhi ṭāyir yusammā kāsir al-ʿiẓām wa-yusammā al-mukallafa ayḍan fa-yurabbīhi], And on the chick cast out by the eagle a bird takes pity, which is named ossifrage and mechalepha, so that it rears it. It is evident that the French orfraye is derived from ossifraga, although among us it denotes something else, namely the haliaeetus or sea eagle. This was observed long ago by Belon, book 2, ch. 7, On Birds.
